query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

decision.trend: Research on Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys has focused on understanding their microstructure, phase stability, and mechanical properties. Earlier studies have explored the effects of alloying elements, such as Sc, on the microstructure and properties of these alloys. More recent studies have investigated the use of computational models, such as CALPHAD, to predict phase evolution and optimize alloy composition. The trend suggests a shift towards using computational models and experimental techniques to design and optimize Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys for specific applications.
decision.unsolved: The evolution of non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys and its effect on corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior remains poorly understood. The lack of understanding of transformation pathways and evolution from metastable states hinders the development of these alloys for high-performance applications.
decision.why: To investigate the self-formation of compositionally complex surface oxides on high entropy alloys and understand their evolution and effect on corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior. This technique will provide atomic-scale characterization of the surface oxides and enable the observation of their formation and evolution in real-time.
